prompt: A developer asks for an order-of-cost estimate at RIBA Stage 1 for a 12,000 m² office in Manchester. Which approach best meets NRM1 and Level 3 design economics practice?

options.text: Prepare an order-of-cost estimate using appropriate functional units, benchmark rates, and stated assumptions with documented exclusions
Issue a fixed lump sum guaranteed to tender without any elemental breakdown
Measure every item to SMM7 rules from outline drawings
Use only the contractor's last project rate with no location or inflation adjustment

explanation: NRM1 order-of-cost estimates at early stages use functional units and benchmarks with transparent assumptions — a core Level 3 cost planning skill.

distractorExplanations.b: Stage 1 estimates are indicative and cannot guarantee tender outcomes without design detail.
distractorExplanations.c: Detailed measurement is premature at Stage 1; order-of-cost methods apply.
distractorExplanations.d: Benchmarks must reflect project-specific factors and current market conditions.

prompt: At RIBA Stage 2, your elemental cost plan shows superstructure at £18.5m against a £17m budget. The architect proposes value engineering. What is your first professional action?

options.text: Move the £1.5m overspend into the design contingency and revisit the frame at Stage 4
Quantify cost drivers and present options with cost/carbon/function trade-offs
Rebase the client budget to £18.5m and record the increase as a client change
Instruct the structural engineer to redesign the frame to the cheapest section sizes before costing

explanation: Level 3 design economics involves diagnosing overspends, facilitating VE, and revising elemental cost plans with documented rationale. Agreed adjustments are then carried into the updated cost plan.

distractorExplanations.a: Absorbing a known overspend into contingency hides the variance and erodes cover for genuine unresolved risk; it is not value engineering.
distractorExplanations.c: Rebasing the budget without a client decision is not advice; the overspend must be diagnosed and options presented before any budget change.
distractorExplanations.d: Directing a redesign before quantifying cost drivers skips option appraisal; the QS advises on trade-offs rather than imposing specification cuts.

prompt: A PQS is appointed on a design-and-build hospital. The employer's agent requests a cost plan at RIBA Stage 3 aligned to NRM1. Which deliverable is most appropriate?

options.text: An NRM2 bill of quantities measured in full to support the employer's agent's tender pricing
An NRM1 order-of-cost estimate using £/m² GIA rates for each building type and a single risk allowance on the total
An elemental cost plan with sub-element breakdown, quantified where possible, tied to the current design
An NRM3 life-cycle cost plan of maintenance and renewal costs over a 60-year period

explanation: RICS QS cost planning at Stage 3 delivers NRM-aligned elemental cost plans supporting employer budget control.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses NRM2 detailed measurement for works procurement with the NRM1 elemental cost plan required at RIBA Stage 3.
distractorExplanations.b: An order-of-cost estimate is the NRM1 deliverable for RIBA Stages 0–1; Stage 3 calls for a formal elemental cost plan.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses NRM3 maintenance and renewal cost planning with the NRM1 capital elemental cost plan requested at Stage 3.

prompt: Your client's gateway review requires demonstration that the £45m GIA budget is still viable at RIBA Stage 4. Which evidence best supports Level 3 advice?

options.text: The Stage 2 order-of-cost estimate uplifted by the latest BCIS all-in tender price index movement
A schedule of provisional sums and prime cost items reconciled to the client's original budget
A benchmark comparison of £/m² GIA against BCIS projects of similar type, location and size
Updated elemental cost plan with measured quantities where available, reconciled to previous stages

explanation: Stage 4 cost plans integrate measurement progress, design changes, and procurement strategy to confirm budget viability. Reconciliation should also reflect the tender strategy.

distractorExplanations.a: Indexing a Stage 2 estimate ignores two stages of design development; Stage 4 viability needs a measured cost plan reconciled to earlier stages.
distractorExplanations.b: Provisional sums and PC items cover undefined or nominated work only; they cannot demonstrate viability of the whole £45m scheme.
distractorExplanations.c: Benchmarking is a feasibility-stage check; at Stage 4 the design supports measured quantities reconciled to earlier estimates.

prompt: A contractor commercial manager must price a two-stage D&B frame agreement. Stage 1 target cost is £28m. Which commercial management action is most sound?

options.text: Build up target cost from supply chain input, risk register, and preliminaries
Set target cost at the employer's £28m budget and recover any shortfall through second-stage variations
Price preliminaries as a fixed percentage of the first-stage direct works estimate from the last framework job
Lock all subcontract prices at Stage 1 so second-stage tendering of packages is not needed

explanation: Commercial management at Level 3 involves transparent target-cost build-ups and risk-aligned commercial structures. Agreed pain/gain mechanisms then set how any over- or under-run against target is shared.

distractorExplanations.b: Adopting the employer's budget as target without a bottom-up build-up mis-prices risk, and planning to recover via variations is unsound commercial practice.
distractorExplanations.c: Preliminaries depend on this job's programme, site and method; a percentage borrowed from another call-off is not a substantiated build-up.
distractorExplanations.d: Two-stage D&B relies on competitive second-stage package tendering to firm up the target; locking prices at Stage 1 removes that market test.

prompt: An employer asks whether to procure a £6m fit-out as traditional or design-and-build. You are providing design economics advice. What should you compare?

options.text: Benchmark £/m² fit-out rates from BCIS for each route and choose the lower median figure
Whole-life implications, cost certainty, programme, design risk allocation, and tender price dispersion
The consultant fee saving under D&B versus the higher fee scale for a fully designed traditional route
Capital cost only, since cost certainty and design risk are fixed by the JCT form chosen later

explanation: Design economics includes procurement route appraisal balancing cost, risk, programme, and quality.

distractorExplanations.a: BCIS £/m² medians do not capture differences in risk transfer, programme or cost certainty between procurement routes.
distractorExplanations.c: Fee comparison is one input only; route appraisal must weigh cost certainty, risk allocation, programme and tender price dispersion.
distractorExplanations.d: Cost certainty and design risk allocation are the main differences between routes, not something settled later by the contract form.

prompt: BCIS location and tender price indices have moved +4.2% since your last cost plan. The project is 14 months from anticipated tender. What adjustment is professionally appropriate?

options.text: Apply the +4.2% BCIS movement once to the whole cost plan total and treat it as fixed until tender
Apply the general RPI rate rather than BCIS tender prices, since tender prices track retail inflation
Apply an evidence-based inflation allowance to relevant elements with stated basis
Leave inflation out and rely on the contractor's fluctuations clause under JCT Option C

explanation: Cost planners use BCIS or equivalent indices to project tender-time costs with documented assumptions. The allowance should be reviewed at the next stage as the tender date firms up.

distractorExplanations.a: +4.2% is past movement; with 14 months to tender a forward forecast of tender price inflation to the tender date is needed, not a one-off historic uplift.
distractorExplanations.b: Retail price inflation does not track construction tender prices; BCIS TPI or an equivalent construction index is the correct basis.
distractorExplanations.d: JCT fluctuations provisions operate post-contract and are often deleted; a pre-tender cost plan must still forecast inflation to the tender date.

prompt: A university client wants lifecycle cost advice for cladding options: aluminium rainscreen vs brick slip. Which analysis best reflects Level 3 design economics?

options.text: Compare capital cost and construction programme only, as FM costs are budgeted by the estates team
Compare NRM1 elemental capital costs and BCIS benchmarks for each cladding system at Stage 2
Compare capital costs plus manufacturer-quoted maintenance intervals without discounting to present value
Compare capital cost, maintenance, replacement cycles, energy performance, and whole-life cost

explanation: Level 3 design economics integrates capital and operational costs for informed option selection. The comparison should run over an agreed study period (NRM3 / BS ISO 15686-5).

distractorExplanations.a: Whole-life costing brings maintenance and replacement into the option decision; leaving them to the estates budget is not design economics advice.
distractorExplanations.b: This is a capital-cost comparison only; lifecycle advice also needs maintenance, replacement cycles and operating costs.
distractorExplanations.c: Whole-life cost needs verified data discounted to present value over an agreed period; undiscounted marketing intervals misstate lifecycle cost.

prompt: Your elemental cost plan includes a 10% design contingency at RIBA Stage 3. The project manager asks why it remains when design is '80% complete'. How do you respond?

options.text: Explain contingency covers unresolved design, scope, and market risk until tender
Reduce contingency to 2% because 80% design completion leaves only construction-phase risk
Transfer the contingency into the contractor's preliminaries so it is priced at tender
Explain that NRM1 fixes design contingency at 10% for every stage up to contract award

explanation: Design contingencies reflect residual uncertainty and should be managed transparently through stages. It should be reduced only as design maturity is evidenced.

distractorExplanations.b: Design 'percent complete' is not risk retired; unresolved design, scope and market risk remain until tender and justify the allowance.
distractorExplanations.c: Employer design contingency is a client risk allowance; moving it into contractor preliminaries hides it and gives away the client's cover.
distractorExplanations.d: NRM1 does not prescribe a fixed percentage; risk allowances are assessed per project and should reduce as risks are resolved.

prompt: A commercial director on a main contractor framework asks you to review three tender returns for a £12m school extension. Returns range £11.4m–£13.1m. What is your best next step?

options.text: Recommend the lowest return, as framework rates already fix scope and qualifications for all bidders
Analyse scope compliance, qualifications, preliminaries, risk, programme, and resource assumptions
Normalise the three returns to the mean and negotiate the highest bidder down to that figure
Rank returns on preliminaries percentage alone, since measured works rates are fixed by the framework

explanation: Commercial management includes rigorous tender return analysis beyond headline price. Only then should a recommendation be made.

distractorExplanations.a: Framework rates do not neutralise tender qualifications or exclusions; a £1.7m spread signals scope differences that must be analysed.
distractorExplanations.c: Averaging and negotiating against a mean is not tender analysis; compliance, qualifications and risk pricing must be reviewed first.
distractorExplanations.d: Preliminaries are only one component; scope compliance, qualifications, programme and risk all drive the recommendation.

prompt: At feasibility, a client provides 2,500 m² net office area and asks for budget advice in central London. Which functional unit approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Cost per workstation using a national BCIS office median, without a London location factor
Cost per m² NIA taken from net lettable rents in the area, converted at a standard yield
Cost per m² GIA or NIA using relevant BCIS benchmarks with adjustments for specification
Apply the 2,500 m² net area directly to BCIS £/m² GIA rates without a net-to-gross conversion

explanation: Feasibility budgeting uses appropriate functional units with transparent benchmark adjustments. Adjustments should also cover basements and site constraints.

distractorExplanations.a: A national median without a London location adjustment understates central London costs; benchmarks need location and specification adjustment.
distractorExplanations.b: Rents and yields belong to development appraisal and valuation, not construction cost benchmarking for a budget estimate.
distractorExplanations.d: BCIS rates are per m² GIA; applying them to a net area without a net-to-gross adjustment understates the budget.

prompt: A design change adds a rooftop plant enclosure. The architect asks if it is 'free' because the plant was already budgeted. What is the correct cost planning view?

options.text: Treat the enclosure as covered by the plant allowance, since NRM1 groups plant and enclosures in services
Cost the enclosure cladding only, as structural and services impacts are dealt with at Stage 4
Draw the enclosure cost from design contingency without reporting it as a change
Assess incremental cost of enclosure, structural support, access, and services diversions

explanation: Design economics requires incremental cost assessment of changes against baseline allowances. Only costs beyond the base plant allowance are new, but they are not 'free'.

distractorExplanations.a: NRM1 places roof plant enclosures and their structural support in other elements; the existing plant allowance does not cover them.
distractorExplanations.b: Associated structural support and services diversions are part of the incremental cost now, not a later-stage issue.
distractorExplanations.c: Contingency drawdowns should be reported against a priced change; silent use hides scope growth from the client.

prompt: You are preparing a pre-tender estimate at RIBA Stage 4 using approximate quantities. Which document set is essential?

options.text: Coordinated drawings, specifications, provisional quantities, and defined measurement rules
Stage 2 concept drawings and the outline specification used for the order-of-cost estimate
A priced NRM2 bill from a recent comparable project, re-indexed to current BCIS prices
The planning approval drawings and the client's room data sheets without engineering input

explanation: Pre-tender estimates at Stage 4 rely on coordinated design and stated measurement basis. Exclusions should be listed alongside.

distractorExplanations.b: Stage 2 concept information supports an early cost plan, not a Stage 4 pre-tender estimate based on technical design.
distractorExplanations.c: Another project's bill may inform rates, but quantities must come from this project's coordinated Stage 4 design.
distractorExplanations.d: Planning drawings and room data lack the coordinated technical and services design a pre-tender estimate needs.

prompt: A client's cost limit for a refurbishment is £8m. Your order-of-cost estimate is £9.3m at Stage 2. What is the most professional recommendation?

options.text: Proceed to Stage 3 and resolve the £1.3m gap through value engineering after tender
Present options to align scope, specification, or phasing to the budget with quantified savings
Advise the client to raise the cost limit to £9.3m as the estimate reflects market rates
Restate the estimate excluding risk allowances and fees so it can be compared with the £8m limit

explanation: When estimates exceed budget, QS advice includes scoped options to close the gap. Residual risk for each option should be stated.

distractorExplanations.a: Deferring a known 16% gap to post-tender VE risks redesign and abortive cost; options should be presented at Stage 2.
distractorExplanations.c: Recommending a budget increase without exploring scope, specification or phasing options gives the client only one choice.
distractorExplanations.d: Stripping risk and fees to fit the limit misstates the cost; the comparison must be like-for-like with the cost limit.

prompt: On a contractor's scheme, you must set a selling price for a negotiated D&B office. Direct costs are £22m, risk £1.2m, overheads 6%, profit target 3%. What commercial principle applies?

options.text: Apply overheads and profit to direct cost only, holding the £1.2m risk as an unpriced contingency
Add 9% to the £22m direct cost and absorb the £1.2m risk within the overheads percentage
Present a transparent build-up separating cost, risk, overheads, and profit
Set the price at the client's budget and back-calculate the profit margin from the difference

explanation: Contractor commercial management uses structured price build-ups for governance and negotiation. Documented assumptions support negotiation.

distractorExplanations.a: Risk is a real cost the contractor carries; leaving it unpriced erodes margin, so the selling price must include risk as well as OH&P.
distractorExplanations.b: Adding 6% and 3% as a flat 9% and hiding risk inside overheads obscures the build-up and under-prices the risk element.
distractorExplanations.d: Price-to-budget ignores the contractor's cost base; the selling price should be built up from cost, risk, overheads and profit.

prompt: An employer's cost report shows a 6% forecast overrun against approved budget at Stage 4. Under design economics practice, what should the report include?

options.text: Revised budget figure reflecting the overrun, with previous variances reset to zero
Contingency drawdown to absorb the 6% overrun, with an amber RAG status for the period
Elemental comparison to BCIS benchmarks showing the overrun is within market norms
Cause analysis, forecast final cost, mitigations, contingency status, and decisions required

explanation: Employer cost reports at Level 3 enable informed decisions with clear variance analysis.

distractorExplanations.a: Resetting variances breaks the audit trail; reports must show movement from the approved budget and its causes.
distractorExplanations.b: Contingency is not there to absorb a 6% overrun silently; the report must analyse cause and seek client decisions.
distractorExplanations.c: Benchmark comparison does not explain the variance against this client's approved budget or set out mitigations.

prompt: A mixed-use scheme needs separate cost plans for residential and commercial elements for funding purposes. How should you structure this?

options.text: Split elemental cost plans by use with shared infrastructure apportioned on an agreed basis
One blended elemental cost plan with residential and commercial split by GIA percentage at the end
Separate cost plans by use, with all shared basement and podium costs charged to the commercial use
Separate cost plans by use, leaving shared cores and plant out as a landlord cost

explanation: Multi-use schemes require transparent cost allocation between uses and shared elements.

distractorExplanations.b: A pro-rata GIA split after the fact ignores differing specifications per use; funders need use-specific elemental plans.
distractorExplanations.c: Shared infrastructure must be apportioned on an agreed basis, not loaded onto one use, or each funder's figure is distorted.
distractorExplanations.d: Shared cores and plant are real construction costs and must be apportioned, not dropped from both cost plans.

prompt: A project uses target cost with 60:40 pain/gain share. Final cost is £500k below target. How should commercial management treat the gain?

options.text: Pay the full £500k to the contractor as a bonus, as the share ratio applies to overruns but not savings
Apply the agreed share mechanism, document calculation, and adjust final payment
Retain the full saving for the client, as gain share is payable under NEC Option D but not Option C
Hold the gain share until the next framework call-off and set it against any future overrun

explanation: Target-cost commercial management includes correct pain/gain administration. Payment follows the contract terms.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats pain/gain as overrun-only; the agreed 60:40 mechanism splits savings as well as overruns, so the £500k is shared.
distractorExplanations.c: Wrongly limits gain share to Option D; NEC Options C and D both carry a pain/gain mechanism, so the agreed share must be paid.
distractorExplanations.d: Gain share is a project-specific contractual payment; carrying it to another call-off without agreement breaches the contract terms.

prompt: Your client asks for carbon and cost integrated advice at Stage 3 for structural frame options. What aligns with contemporary QS design economics?

options.text: Compare capital cost for each frame and defer carbon reporting to Stage 4 for the BREEAM submission
Compare operational energy and capital cost, since the frame drives the building's energy use
Compare embodied carbon and capital cost for steel, concrete, and timber options
Compare embodied carbon, treating capital cost differences between frames as negligible at Stage 3

explanation: Design economics now commonly integrates cost and embodied carbon in option appraisals. Whole-life implications should be stated alongside.

distractorExplanations.a: Frame choice locks in embodied carbon at Stage 3; deferring carbon to a Stage 4 BREEAM report removes it from the option appraisal.
distractorExplanations.b: Frame choice mainly drives embodied carbon; operational energy depends on envelope and services, not structural material.
distractorExplanations.d: Drops cost from integrated advice; capital cost differences between steel, concrete and timber frames are material and must be quantified.

prompt: A cost plan at Stage 3 shows MEP services at 38% of construction cost versus a 32% benchmark. What is your professional response?

options.text: Reduce MEP rates to the 32% benchmark and carry the 6% difference as a design risk
Accept the 38% because benchmarks are only valid for order-of-cost estimates at Stage 1
Re-allocate builder's work in connection with services into substructure to normalise the ratio
Investigate drivers — plant complexity, sustainability targets, riser strategy — and report findings

explanation: Benchmark variance analysis is a key Level 3 cost planning diagnostic skill. Findings should state the normalisation basis used.

distractorExplanations.a: Forcing rates to a benchmark ignores project-specific drivers; a variance needs investigation, not arbitrary adjustment.
distractorExplanations.b: Benchmarks remain a useful diagnostic at every stage; a six-point variance at Stage 3 must be investigated.
distractorExplanations.c: Moving BWIC out of services to hit a ratio misstates the NRM1 elemental split rather than explaining the variance.

prompt: An employer wants 'cost certainty' before committing to D&B tender. At Stage 4, what realistically can you advise?

options.text: Tender-stage cost plan with defined scope, quantified provisional items, and stated residual risks
Fixed contract sum under JCT D&B, which transfers all variation risk to the contractor
Assurance that the lowest tender will match the cost plan within the design contingency
Certification that the contractor's proposals meet the ERs, fixing the final cost at Stage 4

explanation: Cost certainty advice is qualified by scope definition, procurement route, and residual risks.

distractorExplanations.b: A JCT D&B lump sum still moves with employer changes and relevant events; it does not remove variation risk from the employer.
distractorExplanations.c: Tender outcomes depend on market and bidder pricing; a QS cannot assure that tenders will fall within contingency.
distractorExplanations.d: Contractor's proposals arrive at tender and do not fix final cost; certainty depends on scope definition and residual risk.

prompt: A commercial manager reviews supply chain quotations for a £2m cladding package. One subbie is 20% below others. What should you check first?

options.text: Arithmetic errors in the priced schedule, as a 20% gap usually signals a pricing mistake rather than scope
Scope compliance, exclusions, programme, insurances, technical compliance, and financial standing
Whether the price can be used to negotiate the other three bidders down before award
Programme and resource levels, since large price gaps between subcontractors mainly reflect labour productivity

explanation: Commercial supply-chain review examines price alongside scope, risk, and capability.

distractorExplanations.a: Arithmetic checks are part of review, but a 20% gap more often reflects exclusions or scope gaps that must be checked first.
distractorExplanations.c: Using a low quote to Dutch-auction other bidders is poor practice and skips the scope and capability review.
distractorExplanations.d: Attributes the gap to productivity; scope compliance, exclusions, insurances, technical and financial standing must be checked first.

prompt: RICS Level 3 design economics requires you to explain cost plan evolution to APC assessors. Which narrative is strongest?

options.text: How you priced the final NRM2 bill of quantities for tender, with rates built up from first principles
How the cost plan at each stage matched the client budget without any changes needed
How estimates progressed from order-of-cost to pre-tender with key design decisions and VE
How you managed the final account and agreed variations with the contractor after completion

explanation: APC Level 3 design economics is demonstrated through staged cost plan evolution and advice. Market feedback on pricing strengthens the narrative.

distractorExplanations.a: NRM2 bill pricing shows measurement and pricing skill, not the Level 3 design-economics narrative of cost plan evolution.
distractorExplanations.b: Assessors look for how you advised on change and overspend; a no-change story shows no Level 3 reasoning.
distractorExplanations.d: Final account work belongs to post-contract competencies, not design economics and cost plan evolution.

prompt: A phased office development has Phase 1 funded now and Phase 2 in three years. How should cost planning treat Phase 2?

options.text: Combined cost plan at current prices, with Phase 2 shown as an option to be priced later
Phase 2 shown as a £/m² order-of-cost estimate at today's prices, revisited when funded
Phase 2 priced at Phase 1 tender rates plus the 2% annual CPI target for three years
Separate cost plan with escalation assumptions and interface costs between phases

explanation: Phased developments need stage-specific cost plans and interface cost allowances. Enabling works allowances for Phase 2 should also be included.

distractorExplanations.a: Phase 2 starts in three years; current prices without escalation understate its cost and mislead funding decisions.
distractorExplanations.b: A current-price order-of-cost misses escalation and phase interface costs that affect the overall budget.
distractorExplanations.c: CPI is not a construction tender price index; escalation should use BCIS or similar forecasts, plus interface costs.

prompt: Your employer client requests inclusion of FF&E and loose equipment in the construction cost plan for a hotel. What is correct practice?

options.text: Include as separate cost groups with clear exclusion from building contract scope
Include the loose FF&E in the main contractor's lump sum so it falls under one contract
Exclude FF&E as an operator cost outside the QS remit, noting it in the assumptions schedule
Carry FF&E as a provisional sum inside the contractor's preliminaries for later instruction

explanation: Hotel and fit-out cost planning separates building works from FF&E with clear scope boundaries.

distractorExplanations.b: Loose FF&E is usually procured separately by the operator; folding it into the building contract blurs scope and adds main contractor markup.
distractorExplanations.c: Total project cost advice should carry client-defined FF&E allowances; parking it in the assumptions understates the hotel budget.
distractorExplanations.d: Preliminaries cover site running costs; FF&E is not a preliminaries item and should be a separate cost group.

prompt: A design team proposes reducing floor-to-floor height to save cost. What cost planning analysis is needed?

options.text: Quantify savings in external wall area only, since floor-to-floor height affects cladding quantities
Quantify savings in cladding, structure, and MEP against impacts on services capacity and net area
Apply a standard 3% saving per 100 mm reduction from BCIS and adjust the cost plan
Quantify structural savings and confirm the planning height limit, deferring MEP review to Stage 4

explanation: VE on floor-to-floor height requires cross-discipline cost and performance trade-off analysis. Acoustic performance should also be checked.

distractorExplanations.a: Height reduction also changes structure, risers and MEP distribution space; cladding alone understates the trade-off.
distractorExplanations.c: BCIS publishes no such standard factor; savings must be quantified for this building's elements and performance impacts.
distractorExplanations.d: Ceiling void and services capacity are the main risks of lower heights and must be assessed now, not deferred.

prompt: At tender analysis for an employer, the lowest compliant bid is £410k below cost plan. What is the QS recommendation process?

options.text: Recommend award at once, as a compliant bid below cost plan confirms the estimate was prudent
Reject the bid as abnormally low under the Procurement Act once it is 10% below the cost plan
Review scope gaps, rates, programme, and qualifications; reconcile to cost plan
Revise the cost plan down to the tender figure and release the £410k to the client's contingency

explanation: Post-tender employer advice reconciles tenders to cost plans with compliance checks. Then advise on award or clarification.

distractorExplanations.a: Being compliant on submission does not confirm price sustainability; rates, scope gaps and qualifications need review first.
distractorExplanations.b: There is no fixed 10% abnormally-low threshold; the bidder must be asked to explain its price before any rejection.
distractorExplanations.d: Releasing savings before reconciling scope and rates risks hidden gaps; the tender must be scrutinised first.

prompt: A contractor commercial team must forecast preliminaries for an 18-month city centre rebuild. Which factor is most significant?

options.text: Head office overheads and profit, apportioned on turnover across the 18-month programme
A £/m² preliminaries rate from BCIS for city-centre offices applied to the GIA
Design fees and statutory approvals, as these drive time-related preliminaries on rebuilds
Site logistics, hoarding, craneage, working hours restrictions, and phased possession

explanation: Urban refurbishment preliminaries are heavily influenced by logistics and possession phasing.

distractorExplanations.a: Head office OH&P is a separate pricing item; preliminaries are driven by site-specific logistics and time-related costs.
distractorExplanations.b: Benchmarked £/m² rates ignore programme length and site constraints; preliminaries need a time- and method-based build-up.
distractorExplanations.c: Design fees and approvals are project costs outside contractor's preliminaries; site logistics drive preliminaries cost.

prompt: An options appraisal compares new build vs retention of a 1960s frame. Which cost planning input is essential?

options.text: Investigation allowances, remediation risk, temporary works, and programme differential
New build elemental rates from BCIS, with retention priced as a percentage of the new build cost
Embodied carbon savings of retention only, as cost is assumed to favour new build at feasibility
Demolition and enabling costs for new build, with retention costs taken from the 1960s drawings

explanation: New build vs retention appraisals need full lifecycle and risk-adjusted cost comparison. Operational disruption costs should also be included.

distractorExplanations.b: A percentage-of-new-build allowance ignores the frame's condition, remediation and temporary works risks.
distractorExplanations.c: Carbon is a valid factor, but the cost appraisal still needs investigation, remediation and programme allowances.
distractorExplanations.d: Original drawings are unreliable for 1960s frames; intrusive investigation and remediation risk allowances are needed.

prompt: A client's funders require quarterly cost reports during design. What minimum content meets Level 3 standards?

options.text: Current cost plan total against budget, with commentary limited to items over a 5% threshold
Budget status, design development impact, risk/contingency, forecast final cost, and actions for approval
Cash flow forecast and drawdown schedule, with the cost plan issued only at stage gateways
Committed costs to date and consultant fee invoices, reconciled against the funding agreement terms

explanation: Funder-grade cost reporting during design tracks budget, risk, and required decisions.

distractorExplanations.a: A total-versus-budget figure omits forecast final cost, risk status and the decisions funders need to approve.
distractorExplanations.c: Cash flow is useful to funders, but quarterly reports must also track budget, design change impact and risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Committed costs are a post-contract measure; design-stage reports must forecast final cost and design change impact.

prompt: You are commercial manager on a loss-making project at 70% complete. Forecast final cost exceeds sell value. What is the appropriate action?

options.text: Hold the margin forecast at tender level until the final account is agreed, to avoid a write-down
Submit global claims for all delays to recover margin before reforecasting the cost to complete
Reforecast, identify recovery options, escalate commercially, and document margin mitigation
Cut remaining subcontract packages by 10% through post-award renegotiation to restore margin

explanation: Commercial management includes honest forecasting and structured recovery on distressed jobs. Mitigation should be agreed with site and head office.

distractorExplanations.a: Delaying recognition of a known loss breaches commercial governance; forecasts must reflect the current position.
distractorExplanations.b: Global claims without causation rarely succeed; reforecast first and pursue only substantiated entitlements.
distractorExplanations.d: Squeezing let subcontracts is unsound and damages the supply chain; recovery must be planned and escalated.

prompt: A cost plan element for external works is based on a single vendor quote for paving. What weakness should you flag?

options.text: The quote excludes VAT; recommend restating the external works element gross of VAT for the client
External works should be a provisional sum until the landscape design is complete
Paving belongs in NRM1 substructure, so the element should be moved before review
Single-source pricing lacks competitive market test; recommend benchmark or tender comparison

explanation: Cost planning should challenge single-source pricing with market evidence.

distractorExplanations.a: Cost plans are normally reported net of VAT; the real weakness is that one vendor quote gives no market test.
distractorExplanations.b: Provisional sums suit undefined scope; designed paving should be priced, but from more than one source.
distractorExplanations.c: Paving sits in the NRM1 external works group, not substructure; element coding is not the pricing weakness here.

prompt: An employer's agent asks you to align the cost plan to JCT Design & Build employer's requirements. What linkage is key?

options.text: Cost plan scope and exclusions must mirror ERs, drawings, and stated provisional items
Cost plan should follow the contractor's proposals, since these take precedence over the ERs
Cost plan elements must be renamed to match the JCT D&B contract clauses before tender
Cost plan should mirror the JCT activity schedule format required under the D&B contract

explanation: Pre-tender cost plans must align with contract documentation scope.

distractorExplanations.b: Under JCT D&B the ERs set the employer's scope; the cost plan aligns to them and contractor's proposals do not override them.
distractorExplanations.c: Contract clauses govern administration, not cost plan structure; the key link is scope, exclusions and provisional items.
distractorExplanations.d: Activity schedules are an NEC Option A/C concept; JCT D&B uses a contract sum analysis, and scope alignment matters most.

prompt: A developer requests sensitivity analysis on steel price volatility for a 30-storey residential tower. What do you provide?

options.text: A note of the BCIS steel price index trend over the last five years, appended to the cost plan
Elemental sensitivity on steel package with percentage and absolute impact on total cost
A single steel price uplift of 15% added to contingency, with no scenarios modelled
A recommendation to fix steel prices now through a JCT fluctuations Option A clause

explanation: Design-stage sensitivity analysis quantifies material price risk on total project cost. Impact on funding headroom should be shown.

distractorExplanations.a: Historic index trends describe past movement but do not quantify the impact of volatility on this tower's cost.
distractorExplanations.c: One uplift is not sensitivity analysis; it needs scenarios showing percentage and absolute impact on the total.
distractorExplanations.d: JCT fluctuations Option A covers contributions, levies and taxes only; it neither fixes steel prices nor quantifies sensitivity.

prompt: Commercial management requires you to set a bid strategy for a competitive two-envelope tender. What is sound practice?

options.text: Lead with the most aggressive price, since the price envelope is opened before technical scores
Finalise the price envelope first and adapt the technical solution to fit the target price
Technical compliance first, then price submission with internal walk-away thresholds
Submit alternative technical bids in one envelope with prices, to maximise evaluation options

explanation: Two-envelope tender strategy balances technical compliance with disciplined commercial pricing. A risk review should support the price.

distractorExplanations.a: In two-envelope tenders technical scoring normally comes first, and non-compliant bids may never reach price opening.
distractorExplanations.b: Pricing before fixing the technical solution risks non-compliance and mispriced scope in a two-envelope process.
distractorExplanations.d: Mixing price with technical content breaches two-envelope rules and can invalidate the submission.

prompt: At Stage 2, the client asks for a cost plan using elemental format but design is only massing models. What do you do?

options.text: Provide an order-of-cost estimate instead, as NRM1 permits elemental plans only from Stage 3
Produce an NRM2 trade-based estimate from the massing model, then map it to elements later
Use a comparable project's elemental cost plan rebased by BCIS indices without design adjustment
Prepare elemental cost plan with assumptions per element and flag uncertainty

explanation: Early elemental cost plans are assumption-led with clear uncertainty flags. Measurement should be planned for Stage 3.

distractorExplanations.a: NRM1 formal cost plan 1 is produced at Stage 2; massing-led elemental plans are normal with stated assumptions.
distractorExplanations.b: NRM2 trade measurement needs detailed design; elemental cost planning at Stage 2 follows the NRM1 structure.
distractorExplanations.c: Comparable data is a start, but each element must be adjusted to this scheme's massing, specification and site.

prompt: A PQS advises on abnormal costs for a constrained city site with party wall awards. How should these appear in the cost plan?

options.text: Separate identifiable allowances for party wall, logistics, and restrictions within relevant elements
A single abnormal costs percentage on the total, based on BCIS city-centre adjustment factors
Party wall surveyor fees in professional fees, with physical works left to the contractor's risk
Abnormal costs carried within design contingency so the elemental rates stay comparable

explanation: Abnormal site costs should be explicitly allowed in cost plans with justification. Where not element-specific, they can sit in risk.

distractorExplanations.b: A blanket BCIS location factor does not identify party wall or logistics costs for client decisions on this site.
distractorExplanations.c: Party wall awards often require physical works such as underpinning or monitoring, which must be allowed in the cost plan.
distractorExplanations.d: Hiding known abnormals in contingency erodes cover for genuine unknowns; they should be identified allowances.

prompt: Your cost plan reconciliation shows fittings and furnishings underspent but MEP overspent after tender. What advice follows?

options.text: Hold the pre-tender elemental split and report the total, as the tender sum is now fixed
Rebalance forecast, confirm scope transfers with design team, and update post-tender cost plan/report
Net the fittings underspend against the MEP overrun and report a single net variance figure to the client
Instruct MEP omissions to bring the element back to its cost plan allowance before contract

explanation: Post-tender reconciliation reallocates tender pricing across elements with design confirmation.

distractorExplanations.a: The tender sum fixes price, not element allocations; the post-tender cost plan must reflect tender pricing per element.
distractorExplanations.c: Netting hides why elements moved; scope transfers between fittings and MEP must be confirmed with the design team and reported by element.
distractorExplanations.d: Omitting MEP scope to fit a budget ignores design requirements; rebalance the forecast across elements first.

prompt: A contractor asks the PQS to produce the employer's cost plan and also price the same works commercially. What ethical issue arises?

options.text: Confidentiality only — a non-disclosure clause in each appointment resolves the overlap
No conflict, as the PQS remit ends once the employer's cost plan is issued at Stage 4
Conflict of interest — separate teams or declined appointment needed
Fee transparency — both fees must be disclosed to RICS before accepting the roles

explanation: Independence in employer cost planning conflicts with contractor commercial pricing roles. This protects the client and market fairness.

distractorExplanations.a: An NDA addresses information leaks but not the conflict of acting for both employer and contractor on the same works.
distractorExplanations.b: The PQS normally continues into tender and post-contract; acting for the contractor on the same works is a conflict.
distractorExplanations.d: Disclosing fees to RICS is not the issue; the dual role creates a conflict of interest needing barriers or refusal.

prompt: Design economics at Level 3 includes advising on specification levels. Client wants 'Category A office' but budget suggests 'shell and core'. What do you do?

options.text: Price Category A at shell and core rates, assuming tenant contributions will cover fit-out
Recommend Category B fit-out instead, as it sits between shell and core and Category A
Reduce the Category A specification to fit the budget and record the changes in the risk register
Define specification tiers with cost ranges and facilitate client choice against budget

explanation: Specification advice maps fit-out levels to cost with client-led decisions. Market evidence supports the cost ranges.

distractorExplanations.a: Assuming tenant contributions without agreement understates cost; Category A carries a real premium over shell and core.
distractorExplanations.b: Category B is tenant-specific fit-out beyond Category A, not a cheaper tier between shell and core and Category A.
distractorExplanations.c: Specification downgrades need a client decision on priced options; recording them in the risk register is not consent.

prompt: A cost plan for a data centre must capture redundancy in MEP. Which approach is correct?

options.text: Model N+1 or 2N redundancy costs explicitly in MEP elements with basis of design stated
Apply BCIS office MEP rates uplifted by a standard data centre location factor
Carry redundancy as a percentage add-on in design contingency until the tier is chosen
Model redundancy in the NRM3 renewals plan, as backup plant is a lifecycle replacement item

explanation: Specialist buildings need parameter-driven cost plans, not generic benchmarks alone.

distractorExplanations.b: Location factors adjust for region, not building type; data centre redundancy needs explicit MEP modelling.
distractorExplanations.c: Redundancy level is a core design parameter, not a risk; it must be modelled in MEP elements with its basis stated.
distractorExplanations.d: NRM3 covers maintenance and renewal; the capital cost of N+1 or 2N plant belongs in the NRM1 MEP elements.

prompt: Commercial management on a framework requires pricing call-off works without full redesign. What pricing mechanism is typical?

options.text: Cost reimbursement with a fixed fee, as call-off scope is not known at framework award
Priced schedule of rates or bill of quantities with defined adjustment rules for scope changes
A single lump sum agreed at framework award covering the framework's future call-off packages
Daywork rates under the RICS definition of prime cost as the default basis for call-off works

explanation: Framework commercial management relies on documented rates and adjustment rules.

distractorExplanations.a: Cost-reimbursable call-offs give little price certainty; frameworks normally fix rates with adjustment rules.
distractorExplanations.c: Call-off scope is unknown at framework award, so a lump sum for future call-off packages cannot be priced reliably.
distractorExplanations.d: Daywork is a fallback for work that cannot be valued otherwise; using it as the default removes price competition and certainty.

prompt: An employer requests that consultant fees be included in the project cost plan. How should you treat them?

options.text: Add a fee allowance as a percentage of construction cost within preliminaries
Exclude consultant fees, as NRM1 limits the cost plan to the building works estimate only
Separate consultant and construction cost groups with clearly defined inclusion/exclusion boundaries
Include consultant fees within the main contractor's overheads and profit to report one figure

explanation: Project cost plans commonly separate construction and professional fee cost groups.

distractorExplanations.a: Consultant fees are a separate NRM1 project cost group, not part of contractor preliminaries.
distractorExplanations.b: NRM1 cost plans include project and design team fees as a separate group when the client asks for total project cost.
distractorExplanations.d: Contractor OH&P is a construction cost; merging consultant fees into it double-counts and obscures fee scope.

prompt: Value engineering workshop proposes standardising bathroom pods. What cost planning evidence supports the decision?

options.text: Compare pod unit prices from three suppliers, with traditional bathrooms priced from BCIS rates
Assess pods on embodied carbon and BREEAM credits, leaving cost comparison to the contractor at tender
Compare capital costs only, with crane hire and loading-bay logistics left in the contractor's preliminaries
Compare pod capital cost, programme saving, quality control, and logistics against traditional build

explanation: Pod VE decisions need capital, programme, and logistics cost comparison.

distractorExplanations.a: Supplier price comparison captures capital cost only; programme, quality and logistics drive the net benefit.
distractorExplanations.b: Sustainability is relevant, but the VE decision needs QS cost evidence on capital, programme and logistics now.
distractorExplanations.c: Cranage and logistics change with pods and must be counted in the net comparison, not left as unpriced preliminaries.

prompt: A cost report must explain a £1.1m increase since last month due to cladding specification change. What documentation is expected?

options.text: Change reference, elemental impact, comparison to allowance, and updated forecast
Revised total with a note that cladding costs rose, to be detailed at the next stage
Updated forecast with the increase drawn from contingency, without a change reference
Increase applied pro rata across all elements to keep the elemental ratios consistent

explanation: Cost variance reporting ties changes to design decisions with quantified elemental impact. An approval trail should link the change to the client's instruction.

distractorExplanations.b: A £1.1m movement needs quantified, traceable elemental analysis now, not a note deferred to the next stage.
distractorExplanations.c: Contingency drawdown without a change reference loses the audit trail linking cost movement to the design decision.
distractorExplanations.d: Variances must attach to the causative element (external walls); spreading them distorts the cost plan.

prompt: For APC, you must show commercial management on a £35m civils framework. Which example best demonstrates Level 3?

options.text: Preparing NRM2 bills of quantities for call-off tenders, checked by the commercial director
Leading supply chain negotiations, risk pricing, and margin governance with measured outcomes
Producing monthly cost value reconciliations for the framework, as reviewed by your manager
Explaining the NEC4 pricing options and how pain/gain applies under Options C and D

explanation: Level 3 commercial management is shown through leadership in pricing, risk, and supply chain outcomes. Ideally across multiple call-offs.

distractorExplanations.a: Measurement checked by others shows Level 2 doing, not Level 3 leading commercial decisions and outcomes.
distractorExplanations.c: Producing CVRs for review is Level 2 application; Level 3 needs advice and leadership with outcomes.
distractorExplanations.d: Explaining contract theory demonstrates Level 1 knowledge, not Level 3 commercial management on live call-offs.

prompt: A client wants to compare modular vs traditional construction for a student accommodation block. What cost planning deliverable helps?

options.text: Traditional elemental cost plan with modular priced as a percentage saving from supplier data
Modular supplier quotation compared with BCIS traditional £/m² rates for student housing
Option appraisal with capital cost, programme, factory/offsite assumptions, and risk allowances
Option appraisal on capital cost only, with programme savings left to the development appraisal

explanation: Modular vs traditional appraisals need option-specific costs including logistics and interfaces. Interface costs between modules and site works should be priced.

distractorExplanations.a: Supplier-claimed percentage savings are not an option-specific cost model; modular needs its own priced appraisal.
distractorExplanations.b: Comparing a quote with benchmarks is not like-for-like; transport, cranage, interfaces and risk must be added.
distractorExplanations.d: Programme saving (earlier income) is a key modular benefit and belongs in the cost option appraisal.

prompt: Your Stage 4 cost plan will inform a JCT Intermediate Building Contract tender. Should VAT be in the cost plan?

options.text: Include VAT at 20% within each elemental rate so the total matches the client's cash outlay
Exclude VAT from all reports, as VAT is a tax matter for the client's accountants only
Show VAT at the reduced 5% rate, as JCT IBC works are zero-rated or reduced-rated
Follow client brief — typically show net construction cost with VAT stated separately

explanation: UK cost plans should clearly state VAT treatment per client and funding requirements.

distractorExplanations.a: Rates in UK cost plans are normally net; VAT is stated separately because recovery depends on the client's tax status.
distractorExplanations.b: Clients need VAT treatment stated; non-recoverable VAT is a real project cost and must be visible in reporting.
distractorExplanations.c: VAT rate depends on the type of works, such as new dwellings or conversions, not on the JCT contract form.

prompt: A contractor's cost plan for internal governance shows negative margin at tender stage. What should commercial management do before submission?

options.text: Review scope, risk, efficiencies, and walk-away position; escalate for director approval
Submit at a loss to secure turnover, planning to recover margin through variations and claims
Reduce preliminaries and risk allowances to restore margin before submission without director review
Submit at cost and agree a price increase with the client after award through negotiation

explanation: Pre-submission commercial review includes walk-away analysis and governance on margin. A no-bid decision is a valid outcome.

distractorExplanations.b: Bidding at a loss and relying on claims is unsustainable and should be stopped by commercial governance.
distractorExplanations.c: Cutting allowances to hit margin mis-prices risk; a negative margin needs review and director escalation.
distractorExplanations.d: Post-award price increases outside the contract mechanism are improper and undermine the tender process.

prompt: An employer requests integration of Section 106 and CIL into the project cost plan. How do you treat them?

options.text: Include CIL within NRM1 external works and S106 highway works within substructure
Identify planning obligations separately from construction cost with timing per planning agreement
Exclude S106 and CIL from the cost plan, as they are payable only after practical completion
Carry S106 and CIL within the risk allowance until the planning agreement is signed

explanation: Planning obligations are separately identified in project cost plans with correct timing.

distractorExplanations.a: CIL is a charge, not a construction element; planning obligations sit outside NRM1 building works elements.
distractorExplanations.c: CIL is normally due on commencement and S106 triggers vary; both must be timed per the agreements in cash flow.
distractorExplanations.d: Known planning obligations are defined costs, not risks; they should be separately identified, not buried in risk.

prompt: An employer procures a £40m office via JCT Design and Build 2016. Who carries primary design risk after novation of concept design?

options.text: Contractor for completion of design to meet employer's requirements, subject to ERs and liability caps
Employer retains all design risk without exception
Architect remains solely liable after novation
RICS APC assessor carries design risk

explanation: JCT D&B allocates design completion risk to the contractor within ER framework.

distractorExplanations.b: D&B transfers design completion risk to contractor per contract.
distractorExplanations.c: Novation reallocates design responsibility per deed terms.
distractorExplanations.d: Contract parties allocate design risk, not assessors.

prompt: Under NEC4 ECC Option C, target cost mechanics mean

options.text: Activity schedule lump sum with payment on completed activities and no target
Defined cost plus fee with pain/gain share against agreed target at completion
Defined cost plus fee with no target or share, the contractor carrying no cost risk
Bill of quantities remeasurement with pain/gain share against the tendered total

explanation: NEC Option C combines target cost with defined cost and pain/gain share.

distractorExplanations.a: That describes NEC Option A (priced contract with activity schedule), not the Option C target contract.
distractorExplanations.c: That is NEC Option E (cost reimbursable); Option C adds a target with a pain/gain share.
distractorExplanations.d: Remeasurement against a bill is Option B, and a target with a bill is Option D, not Option C.

prompt: FIDIC Red Book 2017 on an overseas infrastructure job — interim payments are based on

Contractor's monthly statement certified on the Engineer's determination of actual cost plus fee
Measured works per BOQ and contract valuation procedures in Conditions of Contract
JCT-style valuation on gross value less 3% retention, applied by the employer's QS

explanation: FIDIC Red Book interim payments follow contract BOQ and valuation clauses.

distractorExplanations.a: Red Book is employer-designed and remeasured; schedule-of-payment milestones suit Yellow or Silver Book lump sums.
distractorExplanations.b: Red Book payments are measured BOQ quantities at contract rates, not cost-plus; the Engineer certifies measured value.
distractorExplanations.d: FIDIC uses the Engineer's interim payment certificates and its own retention provisions, not JCT valuation rules.

prompt: A two-stage tender is chosen for a complex hospital. Stage 1 typically awards

options.text: Full construction contract on a lump sum, with stage 2 used only for design checks
Design and build contract on a target cost, fixed before any contractor design input
Letter of intent for enabling works, with the stage 2 price fixed on first-stage rates
Pre-construction services agreement with defined prelim design and programme

explanation: Two-stage procurement separates pre-construction engagement from stage 2 price fix. It also defines the scope of stage 2 package competition.

distractorExplanations.a: Stage 1 does not award the main build contract; the construction price is fixed at stage 2.
distractorExplanations.b: Two-stage engages the contractor early for buildability; the price is not fixed before their stage 1 input.
distractorExplanations.c: Enabling works letters may follow, but stage 1 is a PCSA; the stage 2 price comes from package tendering, not first-stage rates.

prompt: JCT Standard Building Contract with quantities — variations are valued using

options.text: Contract valuation rules referencing BOQ rates and fair rates hierarchy
Daywork rates under the RICS definition of prime cost, as BOQ rates are fixed to the original scope
NEC compensation event assessment based on Defined Cost plus Fee
A Schedule 2 quotation agreed in advance, which the JCT makes the default valuation route

explanation: JCT SBC variations use contractual rate hierarchy for valuation.

distractorExplanations.b: Dayworks are the fallback where work cannot be measured; the JCT Valuation Rules start from BOQ rates and pro-rata rates.
distractorExplanations.c: Defined Cost plus Fee is the NEC compensation event method; JCT SBC values variations under its own Valuation Rules.
distractorExplanations.d: A Schedule 2 quotation is an optional route used only when instructed; the default is valuation under the JCT Valuation Rules.

prompt: NEC early warning meetings primarily aim to:

options.text: Agree the cost of compensation events before the Project Manager issues instructions
Notify and mitigate risk events collaboratively before they become compensation events
Record contractor delays so delay damages can be deducted at Completion
Review and accept the contractor's revised programme submitted every four weeks

explanation: NEC early warnings are collaborative risk mitigation, core to contract culture.

distractorExplanations.a: Agreeing CE costs is the quotation process; early warnings flag risks before they affect cost, time or quality.
distractorExplanations.c: Early warning is collaborative risk reduction, not a mechanism for building a delay damages case.
distractorExplanations.d: Programme acceptance is a separate clause 31/32 process; early warning meetings deal with notified risks.

Exceptionally adverse weather as a relevant event, with time but no money under the contract

Early contractor involvement in design, giving buildability input before pricing
Open competition from any bidder, maximising price competition for the client
Competitive price with controlled bidder quality and reduced open-market unknowns

prompt: Under a JCT contract, a liquidated damages rate entered in the Contract Particulars will be upheld if it:

options.text: Protects a legitimate interest and is not out of all proportion to it
Is reassessed by the Employer's QS at completion against the actual loss incurred
Is enforceable only where the employer later proves the actual loss suffered
Is a weekly percentage of the contract sum, capped at a standard JCT 10% limit

explanation: Since Cavendish v Makdessi [2015] UKSC 67, an LD clause is a penalty only if the detriment is out of all proportion to the employer's legitimate interest in timely completion. A genuine pre-estimate of loss still passes, but it is no longer the test.

distractorExplanations.b: LDs are agreed in advance in the Contract Particulars; assessing actual loss at completion is general damages, not liquidated damages.
distractorExplanations.c: LDs are recoverable without proving actual loss; that is the purpose of agreeing a liquidated rate.
distractorExplanations.d: JCT sets no standard LD cap; the rate and any cap are entered by the parties in the Contract Particulars.

distractorExplanations.d: NRM1 is elemental cost planning; NRM2 is detailed measurement.

Leave paving unmeasured as provisional sum

distractorExplanations.c: A blanket percentage has no measured basis; the quantity should be measured to the actual workable area with assumptions noted.
distractorExplanations.d: Defined paving scope should be measured where information allows.

Measuring NIA and IPMS floor areas for apportioning the shopping centre's service charge

distractorExplanations.b: Extra doors of the same type are of similar character; contract rates apply and dayworks is only a fallback where rates cannot.

distractorExplanations.c: A benchmark lump sum is a cost plan tool, not a subcontract BOQ; provisional quantities give a remeasurable pricing basis.

Site management, temporary services, hoarding, and insurances
